reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes OneCoin participation through a signup link and paid token packages while promising repayment within 3–6 months and three- to tenfold capital growth in the first year. It also connects payment and participation with recruitment-based rewards, including first-line partners and multi-generation matching bonuses. The advertised returns, withdrawals, gold backing, and bonuses are not established as delivered.

opening.argument: Judge the presentation in context: the speaker says decisions should follow analysis, acknowledges taking a personal risk, and states that no business is without risk. He also says mining has not begun and that withdrawal testing is still pending. Those admissions matter when assessing whether his forecasts are presented as established results. The evidence supports an optimistic, risky investment pitch, but not a claim that the projected outcomes have already been achieved.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The cited package and token passages describe how participation is supposed to work; they do not show that mining or withdrawals occurred. The slide's repayment and growth figures are projections, while the speaker explicitly says mining has not begun. His risk warning gives the judge reason to read those figures as uncertain expectations, not verified returns.

citations.quote: we buy packages, i.e. we can participate in the mining of coins.
mining has not begun yet.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A risk warning does not undo the solicitation. The presentation connects buying packages to mining participation, says more tokens mean more money earned, and displays repayment within 3–6 months and three- to tenfold growth in a year. Saying mining has not begun underscores that the advertised results are prospective, not demonstrated; it does not turn the paid earning offer into neutral market commentary.

opening.argument: Much of the presentation explains a proposed cryptocurrency operation rather than showing a completed investment: the speaker introduces questions to examine before joining, describes finance lessons with videos, files and quizzes, and explains how participants would track mining and transactions once mining starts. He even admits he cannot explain the technical script in detail. Read as an introductory webinar, its package discussion is part of explaining the proposed system, not proof that its promised outcomes are real.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opposing reading treats explanation of packages as sufficient to settle the video's primary purpose. Yet the speaker identifies academy learning as something buyers receive, and says the exchange is only partially implemented. The cited bonus slide describes a compensation structure; it does not establish that anyone received a matching payout. A careful judge can distinguish teaching the proposed operation from verifying its financial claims.

citations.quote: these packages include learning in the 1Coin academy.
only partially implemented by them.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The lessons are bundled with paid packages that also carry tokens for earning money. The speaker explicitly links accumulating tokens to accumulating coins and earnings, while the signup description directs viewers toward enrollment. An educational component does not change the central paid mining offer, especially when the presentation also advertises returns and recruitment compensation.

opening.argument: The offer includes an identifiable service: priced packages with different levels of academy access, lessons on finance, and tests. The speaker discusses package prices and payment methods openly. The record does not show a completed enrollment, a successful withdrawal, or the promised mining in operation. Nor does it establish that the lessons are fictitious. Those gaps matter: a product sold alongside speculative claims and referral incentives should not automatically be treated as a demonstrated fraud.

rebuttal.rebuttal: Buying a package that includes learning is not, by itself, evidence that the educational service is absent. The first-line bonus is described as conditional on selling packages, and the withdrawal example remains a test awaiting confirmation. The opposing side can identify aggressive commercial claims, but its cited passages do not demonstrate a completed transaction or prove that the advertised service was never provided.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The concern is what viewers are urged to buy, not whether a lesson exists. Packages attach tokens to the education, and the speaker says those tokens lead to more coins and more money. He also describes bonuses tied to first-line package sales. The presentation promotes repayment and capital growth before mining has begun; a completed purchase or proven loss is not necessary to recognize the paid returns pitch.
